title: Stomach Acid
objective: After this level you can explain how the stomach uses strong acid safely.
summary: Hydrochloric acid gives the stomach a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5. Bicarbonate mucus, tight junctions and a lining renewed every 3 to 6 days keep it from digesting itself.

cards.headline: Your stomach is full of hydrochloric acid. Why doesn't it dissolve itself?
cards.body: Special cells in your stomach lining make hydrochloric acid, the strong acid from Level 61. The lining it touches is living tissue. The stomach survives with layers of defense, and one of them is Level 64 in action.

cards.fact: Stomach contents have a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5, thanks to hydrochloric acid.
cards.context: The acid comes from parietal cells in the stomach lining. On Level 63's scale that's firmly acidic, in the neighborhood of lime juice at about 2. The acid earns its keep: it kills much of the bacteria that arrive with your food and unfolds proteins so they're easier to digest.

cards.headline: Defense one: a blanket of base
cards.body: The stomach wall is covered in a thick coat of mucus rich in bicarbonate, a base. The mucus is a physical barrier, and its bicarbonate neutralizes acid that works its way in. Across the layer, the pH climbs: the stomach contents can be as acidic as pH 2 to 3 while the cells of the lining sit near neutral. Neutralization, on duty around the clock.

cards.headline: Defenses two and three: tight seams, fast repairs
cards.body: The cells of the lining meet at tight junctions, sealing the seams so gastric juice can't seep into the tissue beneath. And the surface lining is completely replaced every 3 to 6 days, so the lining is always fresh. Heartburn shows acid out of place: it's the painful burning you feel when stomach acid backs up into the esophagus, the tube from mouth to stomach.

cards.headline: Stomach acid: survived
learned: Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid, about pH 1.5 to 3.5
The acid kills much of the bacteria in food
Bicarbonate mucus keeps the lining near neutral
Tight junctions and fast renewal finish the defense

questions.prompt: Which acid do parietal cells in the stomach lining produce?

options.label: Citric acid
options.rationale: That is the acid in lemons.

options.label: Acetic acid
options.rationale: That is the acid in vinegar.

options.label: Sulfuric acid
options.rationale: That is the acid in a car battery.

questions.explanation: Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid, giving stomach contents a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5.

questions.prompt: How does the stomach's mucus layer protect the lining from its own acid?

options.label: It is so acidic that it outcompetes the stomach acid
options.rationale: The mucus carries a base, not more acid.

options.label: Its bicarbonate, a base, neutralizes acid near the lining
It heats the acid until the acid evaporates
options.rationale: Nothing in the stomach boils acid away.

options.label: It stores the acid until the next meal arrives
options.rationale: The mucus blocks and neutralizes acid rather than storing it.

questions.explanation: The thick mucus is a barrier, and its bicarbonate neutralizes acid, keeping the lining's surface near neutral.

questions.prompt: In Level 54, flaking rust exposes fresh iron to more attack. How does the stomach use fresh surfaces to defend itself instead?

options.label: It coats fresh cells in zinc, which corrodes first
options.rationale: Zinc galvanizing protects iron, not the stomach.

options.label: It lets damaged cells flake off and leaves the gap open
options.rationale: Open gaps would let acid seep in.

options.label: It stops making acid whenever the lining is new
options.rationale: The acid keeps coming; the lining keeps renewing.

options.label: It replaces its whole surface lining every 3 to 6 days

questions.explanation: Rust exposes fresh iron to attack, but the stomach replaces its surface lining every 3 to 6 days, so it stays fresh.
